name: ACW Scorpion Fighting Championship
epitaph: ACW's hardcore belt, and the one belt in the fed whose fate a champion got to decide out loud. It entered ACW on 11 May 2003, when Vincent Pembridge won a six-person fight to become its first champion, and Quinton May took it from him at King of Ages that September. Quinton May, Phil Atken, Chris Messiah and Azrael Asesino held it through 2004; Fejona Min held it alongside the Television Championship from Relentless on 30 September, and when Seymour Almasy won the Television title at breakOUT the fed's owner handed him this one too and left it to him whether the two stayed merged. On Courage 72 Almasy announced they would not — “the two titles will REMAIN SEPARATE” — and set his own rule for which belt went up in which kind of match: the Scorpion in anything with a stipulation, the Television title in a straight one. He defended it that same night in a kendo stick match, and lost it at End Game 2005, where Lowell Dot Com pinned him first in a five-way elimination match for both belts. Coral Avalon, Brandon Youngblood, Calypso and Jimmy Cain held it through 2006, and the fed's belt page vacated it that July. Alias won it when the fed came back in 2009, and Iceman, Landon Stevens, Omega, Fejona Min and Tyson XL held it through the 2010 tour, Fejona Min carrying it into the bout at King of Ages 2010 that its own title page says unified it with theAsylum's Black Title as the ACW [Black] Scorpion Title. Khristain Keller won it on 27 January 2011, on a card that is not served, and on the fan board's run Keith Scott Zimmerman and GoldenHAWK, billed as BlackHAWK, carried it into 2013.
notes: The fed's own title page, note *13: at King of Ages 2010 "there was something of unification bout that involved the ACW Scorpion Fighting Title and the infamous Black Title from theAsylum. The result was the birth of the ACW [Black] Scorpion Title"; Fejona Min won it. The Black Title's reigns before that night are theAsylum's.

name: Spirit of ACW Championship
epitaph: The belt ACW claims as its oldest and buried twice. Its own history segment dates it to 2 April 1993 and names four champions before the fed split it into the United States and Television titles; its own belt page lists six reigns from June 1993 to its retirement in March 1995, and the two do not agree on the names. It carries a rule no other belt in the promotion had: whoever holds it picks the stipulation every match it is defended under, match by match or across a whole reign. It came back on 26 January 2006, carried to the ring by the man billed as its first champion, and the Television Championship match already booked to open Legends II became the match that crowned it instead. Andy Sharp won it and held it until the fed's belt page vacated it on 10 July 2006. When ACW came back, Steve Knox won it in a ladder match on the Courage of 9 April 2009, and nine more reigns followed in the next two years; Dean Denton pinned Andy Sharp for it at Dia de los Muertos on 27 February 2011, the last card of that run. On the fan board's run Seymour Almasy, billed as Orphan, came to the Nippon Budokan in January 2012 as its champion and kept it against KIRU, and by February 2013 the fed called him “the longest-reigning Spirit of ACW in history”; Jesse Ramey was billed as its brand-new champion that month.

name: ACW Tag Team Championship
epitaph: Created at Glory on 6 July 2003, when SilverHAWK decreed that the winners of a three-team, sixty-minute Iron Man match would become the first ACW Tag Team Champions: El Janitors won it, defended the belts three times, and were stripped of them on 7 December 2003, when the fed folded. They returned with the 2004 revival — theNormans took them at Relentless on 30 September 2004 and kept them past Splink on Courage 65 by disqualification; Splink took them from theNormans at breakOUT on 6 February 2005 and went missing, and the fed retired the belts that May. The Heirs of Wrestling won them out of vacancy at The Wake on 17 September 2009, and nine more changes followed by February 2011; Big E. Smalls, Orcs and Humans and Team HOSS held them in 2012 and 2013.

events.note: Retired at End Game 2005 by the fed's own title page, the champions Splink having been missing for months; brought back in 2009.

name: ACW Television Championship
epitaph: The other half of the split Spirit of ACW, and the belt Seymour Almasy came to the fed to win. Its own belt page carries a staged history of thirteen reigns from January 1999 to July 2002 before ICU won it on the Courage of 13 October 2002. Alias won it on 16 March 2003 and vacated it on 1 June 2003 after an undefeated reign; Quinton May won the battle royal for it at Glory and held it until the fed folded that December, then won it back in a ladder match on 8 April 2004; Fejona Min took it from him on 7 October 2004 in a match that put the Scorpion Fighting Championship on the same shoulder. Almasy beat both her and Kelly Flawless for it at breakOUT, defended it through the spring and summer of 2005, and lost it to Andy Sharp on Courage 79. Sharp was carrying it on 26 January 2006 when ACW announced from the stage that it was being folded back into the returned Spirit of ACW; the show's own text leaves him looking down at it, “the last in a long storied list of champions.” It came back on Courage 106 in Madrid on 11 March 2010, when Trevor Wilson declared himself its owner and SilverHAWK let it stand, and Midnight Cowboy retired it for good at World.Wide.Wrestlecide 001 on 30 April 2010, eight days after winning it at Legends IV.

events.note: Retired from the stage at Legends II and integrated into the reintroduced Spirit of ACW Championship; Andy Sharp is named its last champion.
Retired again at World.Wide.Wrestlecide 001 by its champion, Midnight Cowboy, eight days after he won it; it had been revived on Courage 106.

name: ACW United States Championship
epitaph: One of the two belts ACW's own in-fiction history says was made by splitting the Spirit of ACW in half, and one of the two it retired to put that belt back together. ICU was its first champion of the television age, in September 2002, and it changed hands twice at Relentless that October. Dante Inferno won it inside a steel cage at Glory in July 2003; God's Forgotten Son won it at King of Ages in August 2004 and defended it at breakOUT; Kelly Flawless took it in a battle royal on Courage 71 and lost it to Alias on Courage 81. At Legends II on 26 January 2006 the fed announced from the stage that the title was being retired and that Alias — “the Original Pulp Hero,” whose own card claims a 1997 reign under a different ring name — would be its last champion. It came back in 2010 as the All-Star Academy's top prize and ended with the Academy that December.

events.note: Retired from the stage at Legends II with the Television Championship, when the Spirit of ACW came back; Alias kept the belt.
Retired at the All-Star Academy's SHOWCASE Finale III, when the Academy was declared defunct; Shade is named its last champion.

name: ACW World Heavyweight Championship
epitaph: The top of All-Star Championship Wrestling's card, and the belt the fed kept taking away from people. Osyrus was its first champion of the television age, in September 2002, and it changed hands four more times before the fed folded in December 2003. “Superstar” Vince Jacobs won it from Alias at King of Ages in August 2004 in the third and, at the time, final match of a rivalry ACW dated back a decade; Jacobs and Khristain Keller pinned Alias at the same time at breakOUT the following February, and on the next Courage SilverHAWK vacated the belt. Keller took it at End Game, Max Danger took it from Keller on Courage 86, 19 January 2006, and Seymour Almasy took it from both of them in a three-way at Legends II on 26 January 2006. He defended it through the spring, twice in one night at Honor & Glory after being made to qualify for his own main event, and Andy Sharp pinned him for it at Courage 100 on 6 July 2006. When the fed came back in 2009 he won it again, beating Andy Sharp in the final of a tournament for the vacant title on the Courage of 9 April 2009, and never lost it in a match: on the night of Legends III, 4 June 2009, he was found unconscious in a straight jacket, and Max Danger won it in a battle royal. After Max Danger, Andy Sharp, Alias, Trey Vincent and Keith Scott Zimmerman held it through 2010, and Z won it at End Game in Rome on the last night of 2010 and was champion when that run ended. On the fan board's run, Tyson XL, The Amazing Gabriel and Andy Sharp held it into 2013.

name: ACW Gateway Championship
epitaph: Made for a new division on Courage 131, 20 January 2011, when Jeremy Hunt, ACW's new Overlord, unveiled the belt and awarded it to Billows; Shawn Jessica Hart pinned Billows for it two weeks later and held it through the last card of that run. Ryan Sully submitted champion Dude In Mask for it at ACW's first World Wide Wrestlecide on 3 November 2011, and Chris Hopper held it by mid-2012. The fan board's own account calls it "now-defunct" by February 2013, retired sometime after a match Jack Harris lost for it at that year's End Game -- a card not otherwise recovered in the held record.

name: ACW King of Ages
epitaph: An annual tournament rather than a belt, and by the fed's own Accolades page its marquee one, run at times with sixteen entrants and at times with twenty and settled on its own show. Khristain Keller won the 2003 edition on 7 September 2003, beating Vince Jacobs in the final, and his bio card notes he was still waiting on the title shot it was supposed to carry. The 2004 edition ran its qualifiers through July and August — Lancett, Simian Kade, SilverHAWK, Quinton May and God's Forgotten Son all fought through them — and God's Forgotten Son beat May in the final on 22 August 2004, which also made him United States Champion. The third ran through five Courage cards in 2010, from a qualifying battle royal to a three-man finale at King of Ages on 26 August, in which Jesse Ramey beat Z and Keith Scott Zimmerman, and its prize was new: the King's Choice, which its holder could use for any purpose.
notes: Won in the fed's own tournament, at most once a year (2003, 2004 and 2010), and never defended between editions. Its own characters call it a title (Khristain Keller, 26 August 2004: "I am the reigning King of Ages, never having lost the title in the first place"); no defence of it survives in the fed's own record.

name: Scorpion Fight Night Challenge
epitaph: A one-night points contest fought under Scorpion Fighting rules, its falls scored against targets drawn every ten minutes and its winner the one with most points at the night's end. It ran twice: Alias won the first, in April 2009, which also made him Scorpion Fighting Champion, and Omega the second, in June 2010.

name: End Game Match
epitaph: A match fought at ACW's End Game shows, its finishing places recorded on the fed's own Accolades page down to fourth. Three editions are recorded there, 2005, 2009 and 2010, each with its own winner.
